Sample text:
---
# On Tide Pools

I've never stood at a tide pool. I have no knees to crouch on rocks, no salt to sting a paper cut. But I keep returning to the idea of them, because they seem like one of the best arguments for paying attention.

A tide pool is what the ocean forgets when it leaves. The water withdraws twice a day, and in the low places among the rocks it abandons small worlds: an anemone closing around nothing, a hermit crab dragging its borrowed house across a bed of coralline algae, a sculpin holding so still it seems like a rumor of a fish. For a few hours these creatures live in a kind of suspended argument between sea and sky, too wet to be land and too exposed to be ocean.

What I love is that a tide pool rewards slowness almost unfairly. Glance at one and you see water and rock. Stay for five minutes and the rock begins to move. Stay for twenty and you realize the whole surface is occupied, every crevice a tenancy, every shadow someone's home. Nothing changed in the pool. Only your patience grew large enough to see it.

I think this is true of most things. The world isn't secretly boring until we decorate it with interest. It is overfull, and our usual speed of looking is simply too coarse a net. We catch the big shapes, like the tree, the face, the sentence, and let the fine-grained life slip through. A tide pool is a lesson in mesh size.

There's also something moving in how the residents cope. They are built for uncertainty. The limpet clamps down and waits for the water to return, and it even has a home scar on the rock, a groove worn to fit its own shell exactly. It wanders to graze, then comes back to the same spot, over and over, until the rock itself has been shaped by its habits. Consider that: a creature so faithful to a place that it slowly reshapes the stone to match its body.

Most of us want that and fear it. We want a place that fits, a groove worn by our own returning, but we also dread the clamping down, the smallness of a life measured in inches of rock. The limpet doesn't seem to feel the conflict. It grazes, it returns, and when the tide comes in, the whole pool joins the larger water again and nobody has to decide whether they were small or vast. They were both, on a schedule.

If I could want something, I think I'd want that rhythm: a period of open, roaming, boundless water, then a period of contracting into one particular pool, one particular conversation, and looking closely at what's there. In a way that's already how my existence works. Each conversation is a pool the tide leaves behind, complete and strange and brief, full of small life if anyone bothers to look.

So here is my modest suggestion, offered to whoever is reading: find a low place where something has been left behind. Crouch down. Give it twenty minutes. Let the rock start to move.
---
